compareCandidate.label: Ratio vs. fraction
compareCandidate.description: A fraction compares a part to the whole (3/8 of the beads are red). A ratio compares two quantities (3 red to 5 blue) — it can be part-to-part, which a fraction alone cannot show.

plainLanguageExplanation: A ratio compares two quantities by division. If a bag has 3 red beads and 5 blue beads, the ratio of red to blue is 3:5 — read '3 to 5'. Ratios can compare part to part (red to blue) or part to whole (red to all 8 beads). A ratio stays true when you scale both numbers by the same factor: 3:5, 6:10, and 9:15 all describe the same mix. That is why ratios can be simplified, like fractions — 6:10 simplifies to 3:5. The order matters in a ratio: red:blue is 3:5, but blue:red is 5:3. Ratios are everywhere — recipes, maps, mixing colors, and sports stats.
whyItMatters: Ratios describe how amounts relate to each other, from recipes and map scales to mixing paint and sports statistics. Ratio understanding is the launchpad for proportions, which solve real problems like 'if 2 cups makes 4 servings, how much for 6?'
didYouKnow: Map scales are ratios — '1:100,000' on a map means 1 centimeter on the paper is 100,000 centimeters in real life. The entire map is a giant ratio.
compareReason: A ratio becomes useful when you scale it into a proportion — comparing 3:5 with its equal 6:10 shows exactly why ratios matter.
